slides.title: An aquatic salamander samples several physical worlds
body: The axolotl, _Ambystoma mexicanum_, retains an aquatic body form as a reproductive adult. **Mechanoreception** detects mechanical disturbances, whereas **electroreception** detects electric fields. These capacities depend on different sensory organs distributed across the skin, rather than on the conspicuous external gills.

Wang and colleagues compared fluorescently labeled organs in 3-month juveniles and 12-month adults. Neuromasts occurred on the head and trunk, while ampullary organs were restricted to the head. Electric stimulation at 5 or 10 Hz changed locomotion under particular experimental conditions.

Sensory function requires calibrated stimulation rather than inference from the animal’s external appearance. Anatomical localization, nerve recordings and controlled behavioral stimulation provide different evidence for sensory function; none alone identifies every receptor-to-behavior connection.

slides.title: Water movement and electric fields use different organs
body: The **lateral-line system** comprises skin receptors and their nerves that sample the nearby aquatic environment. A **neuromast** is a cluster of mechanosensory receptor cells. An **ampullary organ** contains electrosensory cells recessed beneath a skin opening; the two organ types are anatomically distinguishable.

Wang and colleagues used DASPEI, a fluorescent dye that labels metabolically active receptor regions, to identify organs on juvenile axolotls. Larger neuromasts formed conspicuous groups, whereas smaller ampullary organs occurred around them. Tissue sections independently checked their different internal arrangements.

Fluorescence locates candidate receptors rather than measuring their sensory thresholds. Calling an organ electrosensory requires physiological evidence of responses to weak electric fields, with mechanical stimulation used to distinguish electric sensitivity from water-movement sensitivity.

slides.title: Tail movements accompany changes in female behavior
body: **Hulaing** is the courtship movement in which an axolotl undulates its posterior body and tail. Male movements occur near females and at greater distances. A **spermatophore** is a deposited sperm package that a female can collect through her cloacal opening during internal fertilization.

Rupp and colleagues recorded live pairs overnight and analyzed the first 150 min after darkness. Females had shorter walking bouts and switched more frequently among walking, swimming and pausing while males hulaed. These findings come from a 2026 preprint that has not been peer reviewed.

The live-pair comparison associates male behavior with female activity but does not isolate water movement from odor, touch or other cues. Controlled artificial-tail stimulation and peripheral recordings test narrower parts of the proposed communication mechanism.

slides.title: Three skin-organ classes can be distinguished
body: **Pit organs** are a third lateral-line organ category described in the axolotl, alongside neuromasts and ampullary organs. They must not be confused with every recessed receptor casually described as a pit. Historical anatomical terminology is less specific than the later three-category classification.

Wang and colleagues magnified the mandibular region of 3-month juveniles. Neuromasts produced relatively large fluorescent clusters, ampullary organs appeared as smaller ring-like structures, and pit organs appeared small and comparatively dark. Northcutt independently classified organ architecture with tissue sections and surface preparations.

These distinctions establish recognizable structures, rather than three experimentally proven courtship channels. An organ’s position and staining pattern do not identify its transmitter, behavioral role or electrical threshold. The classification requires morphology together with the physiological literature.

slides.title: Head and trunk contain different receptor mixtures
body: The head and trunk do not provide equivalent sampling surfaces. Ampullary organs occur around head neuromast lines, while trunk skin carries neuromasts without the same ampullary population. This regional difference matters whenever tissue from one body region is compared with another.

Wang and colleagues imaged dorsal, lateral and ventral head surfaces using fluorescent labeling. Their 3-month juveniles had ampullary organs in head regions including the snout and jaws, but not on the imaged trunk. Northcutt’s anatomical preparations also separated head receptor fields from trunk lines.

A regional expression difference may reflect different receptor populations or other skin cells. It cannot automatically be assigned to an ampullary receptor cell. Head-versus-trunk comparisons therefore constrain localization without providing the cellular specificity of an isolated-receptor experiment.

slides.title: Sensory epithelia contain receptors and support cells
body: A **sensory epithelium** is an organized cell layer containing receptor cells and associated supporting cells. Northcutt examined axolotl neuromasts and pit organs in sections and surface preparations, distinguishing sensory cells from the surrounding tissue rather than classifying organs by external appearance alone.

Microscopic sections reveal organized receptor groups and different relationships to the skin surface. Neuromast sensory cells carry apical specializations, meaning specializations at their water-facing ends. The cellular arrangement is therefore more informative than the simple presence of a skin opening.

Histology, the microscopic study of tissue structure, identifies the location and arrangement of cells. It does not measure how a membrane channel opens or how rapidly a nerve fires. Those mechanisms require physiological recordings or interventions in an appropriately identified preparation.

slides.title: An ampullary canal links water to recessed receptors
body: An ampullary organ contains receptor cells below the epidermal surface, connected to the environment through a canal. The **epidermis** is the outer skin layer. This arrangement differs from an exposed mechanosensory cluster, even though both belong to the lateral-line system.

Wang and colleagues examined juvenile head skin in vertical and horizontal sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin. Ampullary organs appeared as rounded compact groups; vertical sections located the pore and recessed cavity, while horizontal sections distinguished the clustered receptor region from surrounding skin.

The canal provides an anatomical route between water and sensory tissue. The sections do not directly measure canal resistance, receptor current or channel identity. Their mechanistic contribution is to locate the specialized cells that electrical recordings and molecular assays must subsequently interrogate.

slides.title: Neuromasts place mechanical receptors near the surface
body: Neuromasts organize **hair cells**, sensory cells with apical projections responsive to mechanical input, in clusters close to the skin surface. Their name refers to these cellular specializations rather than mammalian hair. They are structurally distinct from the compact recessed ampullary organs.

Wang and colleagues compared matched head-skin sections. Neuromasts formed larger spindle-shaped receptor clusters in horizontal sections and had sensory projections extending outward in vertical sections. Using the same staining and tissue-processing methods limited procedural differences between the two organ categories.

Water displacement can be converted into a change in receptor activity and then into nerve impulses. These sections establish where that conversion occurs, but do not identify every mechanotransduction channel. Mechanical sensitivity must be supported by recordings during calibrated water-motion stimulation.

slides.title: Peripheral nerves connect distinct receptor fields
body: An **afferent** carries sensory information toward the central nervous system. Northcutt traced lateral-line nerves and their terminal fields in axolotl skin, linking receptor positions to identifiable nerve branches rather than assuming that adjacent receptors share identical innervation.

Whole-mount preparations preserve branching relationships across the head. The anterodorsal and anteroventral lateral-line nerves supply different territories, including receptor groups around the snout and jaws. Tissue anatomy distinguishes these sensory pathways from other cranial nerves passing through nearby regions.

A nerve recording samples only the receptors served by the recorded branch. Responses from a dorsal snout branch cannot be generalized to every neuromast or ampullary organ on the animal. The anatomical field establishes the spatial meaning of the physiological signal without specifying its behavioral interpretation.

slides.title: Receptor maturation can be followed across development
body: A **developmental stage** describes anatomical maturity rather than a fixed number of days. Modrell and Baker labeled living axolotl embryos with DASPEI and examined receptor cells at stages 40, 42 and 44. Neuromasts were already visible at stage 40 and became more extensive thereafter.

The authors also used antibodies against **parvalbumin-3**, a calcium-binding protein expressed in sensory hair cells. Neuromasts contained more labeled receptor cells than individual ampullary organs in their examples. The complementary stains separated organ appearance from receptor-cell identity.

DASPEI did not label ampullary organs under that study’s short-incubation conditions, although later protocols detected their fluorescence. Failure of one stain is therefore not evidence that the organ is absent. Neither labeling method directly measures the developmental onset of a complete courtship response.

slides.title: Eya4 marks both mechanical and electrical receptor cells
body: **Eya4** is a gene encoding a transcriptional coactivator, a protein that helps regulate gene expression. Modrell and Baker used **in situ hybridization**, a method that locates a selected RNA within tissue, to identify Eya4-expressing cells in larval axolotl sensory organs.

Eya4 signal occurred in both neuromasts and ampullary organs. Combining RNA localization with parvalbumin-3 labeling and nuclear staining restricted the signal to receptor cells rather than the surrounding support-cell population. Sections provided an independent view of this cellular localization.

A shared developmental marker is compatible with related cellular origins. It does not make the two receptor types functionally interchangeable. Eya4 is not an electrical transduction channel, and expression alone does not establish that the gene is necessary for sensory activity in either organ.

slides.title: Lateral-line placodes establish sensory territories
body: A **placode** is a localized thickening of embryonic surface tissue that contributes to a sensory organ or its associated neurons. Modrell and Baker followed Eya4 expression as the axolotl lateral-line placodes, receptor lines and sensory ganglia developed.

At stage 28, prominent expression occurred in the developing ear region. By stage 33, lateral-line placodes also expressed Eya4; stages 38–39 included receptor lines and their ganglia. A **ganglion** is a collection of neuronal cell bodies outside the central nervous system.

The facial-nerve ganglion beside a lateral-line ganglion did not share the same Eya4 signal. This spatial comparison supports selective localization, rather than indiscriminate neuronal staining. Developmental expression maps constrain tissue identity but do not prove how mature electrical or mechanical signals are processed.

slides.title: Sensory afferents occupy ordered hindbrain territories
body: The **hindbrain** is the posterior brain region that receives several cranial sensory inputs. Fritzsch and colleagues labeled different axolotl sensory nerves with distinguishable dyes, identifying the central territories reached by the ear, mechanosensory lateral line and ampullary organs.

The adult organization placed inner-ear afferents more ventrally, mechanosensory lateral-line afferents above them, and ampullary projections most dorsally. **Dorsal** and **ventral** specify anatomical directions. The dye combinations provided direct anatomical comparisons between pathways within a preparation.

Spatial segregation establishes distinct central input territories, not a complete wiring diagram for behavior. A dye-labeled projection does not reveal the transmitter at every synapse or which downstream cells cause orientation. The developmental sequence provides a separate test of how the ordered arrangement emerges.

slides.title: Central pathways appear in a developmental sequence
body: Fritzsch and colleagues traced central sensory projections in axolotl embryos at successive stages. A **fascicle** is a bundle of nerve fibers. Comparing the bundles at matched developmental stages tested whether sensory pathways initially overlap or instead occupy distinct territories as they appear.

Trigeminal projections were detectable at stage 32, inner-ear projections at stage 34, and additional mechanosensory lateral-line bundles at stage 36. Later bundles lay more dorsally. Dye tracing preserved their entry sites and extensions within the hindbrain, rather than inferring position from peripheral receptor anatomy.

The temporal sequence is consistent with later afferents entering still-unoccupied dorsal territory. It does not establish that timing alone determines projection identity. Molecular recognition and other developmental processes remain possible contributors because the study did not experimentally exchange the arrival times of different pathways.

slides.title: Electrical responsiveness emerges with later projections
body: An anatomical pathway can develop before a complete sensory behavior is measurable. Fritzsch and colleagues combined dye tracing with preliminary responses to brief electric stimulation in developing axolotls, distinguishing early and late animals within stage 38.

Stage 37 and younger embryos lacked the tested curling response. Early stage-38 animals had mechanosensory projections but no additional traced ampullary projection; late stage-38 animals exhibited a more dorsal fiber population and responded with a lateral flexion progressing into a head-to-tail curl.

The correspondence supports coordinated peripheral and central maturation. It does not identify the exact field threshold or prove that the newly traced fibers alone generate curling. The developmental association is stronger than anatomy alone, but remains different from selectively removing the ampullary pathway and testing the response.

Early stage-38 animals had mechanosensory projections but no additional traced ampullary projection; late stage-38 animals exhibited a more dorsal fiber population and responded with a lateral flexion progressing into a head-to-tail curl.

The authors interpreted the additional dorsal fibers through their correspondence with adult organization. This is an anatomical identification supported by developmental timing, rather than direct recording of each labeled axon’s electric response.

The correspondence supports coordinated peripheral and central maturation. It does not identify the exact field threshold or prove that the newly traced fibers alone generate curling. The developmental association is stronger than anatomy alone, but remains different from selectively removing the ampullary pathway and testing the response.

slides.title: Single ampullary afferents branch within an organ
body: Peripheral wiring limits what a nerve impulse represents. Fritzsch and colleagues filled fibers in the superficial ophthalmic branch at stage 40, when the axolotl projection pattern was more adult-like. The preparation linked individual peripheral axons to the receptor organs they supplied.

Larger neuromasts received multiple afferents, whereas an individual ampullary organ received a single branching afferent reaching its sensory cells. **Branching** allows one axon to contact more than one receptor cell. The dye fills retained these contacts and the surrounding peripheral nerve course.

This difference suggests different degrees of convergence before signals reach the brain. It does not specify how many synapses are functionally active or the electrical gain of each contact. A single afferent’s discharge reflects its connected receptor population, rather than providing separate measurements from every receptor cell.

slides.title: Weak-field thresholds separate sensory fiber classes
body: Münz and colleagues recorded impulses from an axolotl head lateral-line nerve while applying calibrated electric fields. A **threshold** is the smallest tested stimulus sufficient to produce the defined response. Their square pulses lasted 500 ms, allowing response changes to be compared with baseline discharge.

One class of units responded below approximately 100 µV/cm. Other units required fields above 3 mV/cm and were mechanically sensitive. The large difference separates specialized weak-field detection from activation by much stronger electrical stimulation; electric responsiveness alone is insufficient to classify a receptor.

The units came from a nerve containing multiple sensory fibers. The recordings establish peripheral electroreception but did not directly label each recorded ending. Later anatomical classifications identify ampullary organs more specifically than the historical description of small head pit organs.

slides.title: Electric polarity changes the direction of discharge
body: A peripheral electroreceptor can encode electric-field direction through an increase or decrease in ongoing activity. Münz and colleagues compared the same recorded unit during electric square pulses with opposite polarities, using prestimulus discharge as its reference condition.

When the electrode near the snout became negative, electrosensory discharge increased. Reversing the field reduced discharge. Responses to 500-ms pulses varied with field strength, so a change in impulse rate carried information about both stimulus polarity and magnitude within the tested range.

A decrease in firing is a sensory response rather than a failure to detect the stimulus. These nerve recordings do not identify the receptor’s membrane current or distinguish every synaptic step. They describe the output signal already transmitted through the afferent pathway.

slides.title: Slow electric oscillations modulate afferent firing
body: **Phase locking** means that impulses occur at a reproducible part of a repeating stimulus cycle. Münz and colleagues applied sinusoidal electric fields, smoothly alternating fields whose frequency is measured in hertz, or cycles per second, to peripheral axolotl nerve units.

Electrosensory impulses followed low-frequency stimulation from approximately 0.1 to 7 Hz. Above 7 Hz, impulses no longer accompanied every cycle, although overall activity could remain modulated up to 25 Hz. Mechanical stimulation at tested water-displacement amplitudes did not reproduce this weak-field response pattern.

The decline in cycle-by-cycle following separates timing precision from the continued detection of stimulation. The preparation establishes peripheral frequency dependence, not a behavioral preference for a particular frequency. A female’s response to a moving courtship tail also cannot be inferred from electrical tuning.

slides.title: Juveniles increase movement under a tested electric field
body: Wang and colleagues tested freely moving 3-month axolotls in a tank containing a dipole electrode pair, two nearby electrodes generating a spatially varying electric field. Opaque barriers limited visual cues, and trials without stimulation provided the basal behavioral comparison.

With an applied electrode voltage of 2 V at 5 Hz, juveniles traveled farther and occupied a broader region than during basal trials. Their mean distance from the electrode pair did not show the corresponding directional reduction observed in the adult comparison.

Increased locomotion establishes an electric-stimulation-associated behavioral change under these conditions. It does not by itself establish attraction to the source. Total path length and position relative to the electrodes answer different questions, and electrode voltage is not the field strength at the animal’s receptor surface.

slides.title: Adults move closer to the electric source
body: **Electrotaxis** is directional movement in relation to an electric field. Wang and colleagues compared basal behavior with electric stimulation in 12-month axolotls, using the same positional measurements applied to juveniles. The adult test included a 1-V, 10-Hz electrode stimulus.

Adults increased total travel distance and reduced their average distance from the electrode pair. The combination indicates more locomotion together with movement toward the region of stronger field. It differs from the juvenile 2-V, 5-Hz condition, which primarily increased locomotion without a detected decrease in radius.

The comparison does not isolate age as the sole causal factor because stimulus parameters also differed. It supports source-directed behavior in the adult preparation, rather than a universal developmental rule or evidence that natural courtship involves electric-field attraction.

slides.title: Electrode voltage is not a receptor threshold
body: An **electric-field gradient** describes spatial variation in voltage per unit distance. A generator voltage specifies the difference across electrodes; the field at an axolotl depends on electrode geometry, water conductivity and the animal’s position. These quantities have different units and meanings.

Wang and colleagues calibrated the tank field with recording electrodes separated by 1 cm. Field intensity declined with distance from the stimulating pair. Their 5-Hz juvenile and 10-Hz adult assays tracked movement through this nonuniform environment rather than holding receptor stimulation constant.

The 2-V behavioral condition cannot be numerically equated with the approximately 100-µV/cm peripheral thresholds in the earlier nerve study. A controlled threshold requires a known field at the receptor and a defined response criterion; free movement changes both stimulus exposure and behavioral measurement.

slides.title: Regional transcriptomes remain mixtures of cell types
body: A **transcriptome** is the set of RNA transcripts recovered from a tissue. Wang and colleagues compared head skin containing ampullary organs and neuromasts, trunk skin containing neuromasts, and fin tissue without the sampled lateral-line receptors. These were regional tissue preparations rather than isolated receptor cells.

**Principal-component analysis** summarizes major patterns of variation across measured genes. The three tissue groups separated in the reported analysis, indicating systematic differences in their RNA profiles. Matched processing and biological replication supported the reproducibility of this regional contrast.

Separation does not identify the cell type responsible for a particular transcript. Skin regions differ in many components besides sensory receptors. An ampullary-enriched candidate therefore requires cellular localization or functional recording before its expression can be assigned specifically to electric transduction.

slides.title: Receptor-associated genes enrich sensory skin regions
body: A **marker gene** is a gene whose expression helps identify a tissue or cell population. Wang and colleagues measured previously reported sensory-associated genes across head skin, trunk skin and fin. Their marker panel included Eya4 and genes associated with receptor development or synaptic function.

The published heat map represents relative expression within each gene, with head and trunk receptor-containing tissues generally differing from fin. Some genes were especially enriched in head skin, while others favored neuromast-containing trunk tissue. This patterned distribution is more specific than an overall RNA abundance difference.

A marker panel supports the presence of sensory tissue in the preparation. It does not establish that every enriched gene is an electroreceptor transduction molecule. The head sample includes neuromasts, ampullary organs and nonsensory cells, so physiological attribution remains a separate problem.

slides.title: Vesicular glutamate machinery is a synaptic candidate
body: **Glutamate** is a neurotransmitter, a chemical used in communication between cells. The gene **Slc17a8** encodes VGLUT3, a transporter that packages glutamate into synaptic vesicles. A **vesicle** is a membrane-bound compartment that can release its contents at a synapse.

Wang and colleagues found Slc17a8 enrichment in receptor-containing tissues and checked selected marker differences using **quantitative PCR**, a method estimating the abundance of selected RNA-derived sequences. Head skin had particularly high expression of Slc17a8 within the reported regional comparison.

The finding is consistent with glutamatergic machinery in sensory tissue, but does not directly measure transmitter release. It also does not identify the postsynaptic glutamate receptor or its current. Assigning a specific receptor-to-afferent synapse requires cell-resolved localization and physiological tests beyond tissue RNA.

slides.title: Kv transcripts nominate membrane mechanisms
body: A **voltage-gated potassium channel**, abbreviated Kv, changes its probability of opening with membrane voltage and permits potassium-ion movement. Such channels can shape the electrical response of a cell. Identifying a channel transcript is therefore relevant to excitability, but is not itself a recording of channel activity.

Wang and colleagues compared potassium-channel-related gene expression across mixed head, trunk and fin tissues. Several Kv-associated transcripts were enriched in the head sample. Kcna5, encoding the Kv1.5 channel, was particularly elevated relative to the other sampled regions.

These findings nominate molecular candidates for electroreceptor physiology. They do not prove that Kv1.5 produces electric sensitivity or that its current has a specific magnitude in an ampullary cell. The mixed-tissue assay cannot exclude contributions from neighboring cells or other excitable structures.

slides.title: Broad potassium-channel inhibition changes behavior
body: **4-Aminopyridine**, or 4-AP, inhibits multiple voltage-gated potassium channels. Wang and colleagues immersed juvenile axolotls in 100 µM 4-AP for 30 min, then tested their behavior in fresh water. The comparison used basal and electric-stimulation trials rather than assuming that the drug itself was a sensory stimulus.

Untreated juveniles increased path length during the 2-V, 5-Hz stimulus. The corresponding increase was absent after 4-AP exposure. Position maps and movement measurements therefore linked a broad channel intervention to the electrically evoked locomotor effect.

The intervention supports a potassium-channel contribution somewhere in the tested pathway. Whole-animal exposure cannot localize the effect to ampullary cells or select Kv1.5 alone. Changes in peripheral, central or motor excitability remain alternatives even when baseline behavior appears broadly preserved.

slides.title: Baseline behavior constrains drug interpretations
body: A pharmacological effect on sensory behavior can reflect impaired detection, altered processing or a general motor deficit. Wang and colleagues tested adult axolotls after 30-min exposure to 200 µM 4-AP, comparing their electric-stimulation responses with untreated adults and basal behavior.

After treatment, the 1-V, 10-Hz stimulus no longer produced the detected increase in path length or reduction in distance to the electrode source. The authors reported no obvious changes in basic physiological activity, survival or feeding under the tested exposure conditions.

Those observations argue against gross incapacitation, but do not establish complete motor equivalence or receptor-specific inhibition. A selective ampullary intervention and direct receptor recording would be required to assign the behavioral effect to one channel subtype at one cellular site.

slides.title: Midbrain units receive more than one sensory modality
body: The **optic tectum** is a midbrain structure receiving sensory information relevant to spatial behavior. Bartels and colleagues recorded axolotl units during mechanical water displacement, weak electric fields, visual stimulation and acoustic or vibrational stimulation. Electrode positions were verified with anatomical measurements and histology.

Many units responded to more than one modality, while other units responded to only one tested stimulus category. **Multimodal** means responsive to multiple kinds of sensory input; it does not imply that all inputs have identical sensitivity or identical response timing.

Convergence provides a physiological substrate for comparing aquatic cues. It does not demonstrate that every responsive unit controls prey capture or courtship. The recording identifies sensory access to a central population, rather than a complete causal chain from a particular natural signal to an action.

slides.title: Different modalities reach units with different latencies
body: **Response latency** is the interval between stimulus onset and the measured neuronal response. Bartels and colleagues compared axolotl midbrain responses to several sensory modalities while maintaining defined stimulation and recording conditions. The comparison separates rapid access to a unit from the total strength of its response.

The shortest visual latencies were approximately 8–17 ms. Lateral-line and vestibular responses occurred after approximately 35–58 ms, while electrosensory responses occurred after approximately 79–150 ms. **Vestibular** inputs concern the inner-ear system associated with bodily movement and orientation.

These preparation-specific ranges indicate unequal response timing. They do not measure behavioral reaction time or the number of synapses in each pathway. slides.title: Spatial maps overlap incompletely across modalities
body: A **topographic map** preserves a systematic relationship between stimulus position and neuronal position. Bartels and colleagues varied the direction of water-surface and electric-field stimulation while recording at different locations in the axolotl tectum. Histological verification connected response properties to the sampled anatomy.

Electrical units and many mechanical units were direction-selective, responding preferentially to particular stimulus directions. Each tectal hemisphere represented the opposite side of surrounding space. The electrosensory, mechanosensory and visual maps aligned only partly, with poorer correspondence in caudal regions.

slides.title: Efferent fibers carry signals back toward sensory organs
body: An **efferent** carries signals away from the central nervous system toward peripheral targets. Münz and Claas recorded lateral-line efferents in head and trunk nerve branches, separating these outgoing fibers from sensory afferents. They analyzed baseline discharge and responses to controlled stimulation.

Individual efferents discharged irregularly, and bursting was common. **Bursting** means groups of impulses separated by quieter intervals. Units within the same nerve branch differed in their baseline patterns, so the peripheral pathway did not receive one uniform ongoing command.

The recordings establish active central feedback to the lateral-line periphery. They do not directly measure the effect at a receptor synapse or identify its transmitter and receptor molecules. A discharge pattern in an outgoing axon must be distinguished from the resulting change in sensory-cell gain.

slides.title: Movement coincides with recruitment of efferent activity
body: An animal’s movement produces water disturbances that can stimulate its own lateral line. **Reafference** is sensory input generated by the animal’s own action. Münz and Claas examined whether lateral-line efferent activity changed during axolotl movements in their recording preparation.

Movements were accompanied by recruitment of additional efferent units and altered discharge patterns. The authors monitored movement alongside nerve impulses, retaining the timing relationship rather than inferring motor association from baseline activity alone. Multiple units could participate within a single peripheral branch.

This association is compatible with regulation of self-generated sensory input. It does not prove subtraction of reafference, nor identify a motor-command copy at a particular synapse. Directly measuring afferent consequences during controlled efferent manipulation would be required to establish that specific computational mechanism.

slides.title: Several sensory inputs modulate central feedback
body: Münz and Claas stimulated different sensory systems while recording axolotl lateral-line efferents. Visual, labyrinthine, somatosensory and mechanical lateral-line stimulation could change outgoing activity. **Somatosensory** input concerns bodily touch or related stimulation; labyrinthine input arises from inner-ear sensory structures.

Visual stimulation could produce strong changes when illumination was switched on or off. By contrast, tested electrosensory stimulation did not alter efferent firing. Comparing modalities within the preparation limits the assumption that every detected environmental event automatically recruits the same feedback pathway.

Neither the visual nor mechanical effects identify the neurotransmitter responsible at the peripheral target, which was not assayed in these recordings.

slides.title: Lesions separate distributed inputs from local pathways
body: A **lesion** is a localized interruption or removal of neural tissue. Münz and Claas made lesions at different central levels while monitoring axolotl efferent activity. This approach tested which regions were required for particular inputs to continue reaching the outgoing lateral-line pathway.

Baseline activity depended on inputs distributed across multiple brain levels, extending to the diencephalon. Mechanosensory input could be mediated at the medullary level, a hindbrain region. Individual efferent fibers also supplied different peripheral fields and conducted impulses at approximately 5–12 m/s.

slides.title: A physical Robotail isolates courtship motion parameters
body: Rupp and colleagues constructed a **Robotail**, a physical model driven to reproduce male axolotl tail movements. The model separated sweep angle, elevation and movement speed, variables that naturally change together during courtship. This study is a 2026 preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

Behavioral tests included sweeps of 10°, 30° and 90° and speeds of 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 Hz, with elevation varied separately. The apparatus used a tail shape derived from measured animals rather than treating every water disturbance as an equivalent courtship signal.

The manipulation provides control over physical movement while retaining a simplified sender. It does not reproduce all cues of a live male or establish that females recognize the model as a conspecific. Behavioral responses must therefore be interpreted with the chemical context and the measured response category specified.

slides.title: Chemical context changes responses to a moving tail
body: A moving object can carry different biological meanings depending on accompanying cues. In the Rupp preprint, females initially attacked the Robotail as if it were prey. The investigators added **whole-body odorants**, a mixture collected from male-conditioned water, to provide a chemical context.

Male odorants reduced attacks and nipping but did not eliminate all aggressive contacts. Under that context, females also nudged the tail and changed walking bouts, proximity and locomotor transitions as physical movement parameters varied. The observations separate specific interaction measures from undifferentiated activity.

The manipulation does not identify which molecule changed behavior, nor prove that a single pheromone was necessary. Because the odor stimulus was a mixture, the inference concerns chemical context accompanying mechanical motion. The findings remain preliminary because the source has not been peer reviewed.

slides.title: A snout nerve records responses to physical tail motion
body: The **anterodorsal lateral-line nerve**, or ADLLn, serves receptors on the dorsal snout. Rupp and colleagues recorded this nerve in a female axolotl preparation placed beneath the Robotail, approximating the snout-to-tail arrangement during following. The report is a preprint, not a peer-reviewed finding.

A suction electrode collected **multiunit** activity, impulses from more than one fiber. Each test included a 15-s preparation period and 30-s stimulation period, with 2 min between trials. The authors rotated stimulus order and held tail elevation near 45° during these recordings.

The activity establishes peripheral access to movement-related stimulation in the sampled nerve. The preparation did not perform courtship behavior during recording, and the mixed signal does not identify a complete central decision circuit. Anatomical targeting and response timing constrain the sensory interpretation without proving behavioral necessity.

slides.title: Sweep angle changes the peripheral response
body: Rupp and colleagues measured **firing rate**, the number of detected nerve impulses per second, before and during Robotail movement. They expressed stimulation responses relative to each preparation’s baseline. This normalization compared response changes rather than assuming identical baseline firing across animals.

Female ADLLn activity increased during all three tested sweep angles. A 30° sweep produced a stronger relative response than a 10° sweep, while the 90° comparison did not establish a corresponding reliable increase. Speeds of 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 Hz all evoked activity.

The peripheral response was not a simple monotonic function of movement width. Neither normalized firing nor one response maximum is a direct measure of attractiveness. slides.title: Behavior and nerve responses favor different motions
body: **Sender–receiver matching** proposes that signal production and receiver sensitivity become aligned. **Receiver bias** proposes that pre-existing sensory or behavioral preferences influence signal evolution. Rupp and colleagues compared natural male motions with female behavioral and nerve responses to the Robotail in a non-peer-reviewed preprint.

A 30° sweep at 1.0 Hz was common in male production and produced a stronger female nerve response than the narrow, slow 10°/0.5-Hz reference. Female locomotor transitions increased more clearly for combinations including 30°/1.5 Hz, 90°/1.0 Hz and 90°/1.5 Hz.

Peripheral sensitivity and behavioral responsiveness therefore emphasized different combinations. This is compatible with different processing stages rather than a contradiction. The experiment does not establish the historical evolutionary origin of the signal, and strong state switching is not equivalent to enhanced mating success.

slides.title: Courtship water contains distinctive secreted proteins
body: A **pheromone** is a chemical signal exchanged between members of the same species that changes physiology or behavior. Maex and colleagues analyzed water from courting axolotl pairs and compared it with water from noncourting males and noncourting females, controlling for ordinary animal-conditioned water.

**Chromatography** separates molecules according to their interactions with a column and solvent. Courtship water contained distinctive protein peaks. Gel separation identified multiple proteins near 20–25 kDa, where a kilodalton is a unit of molecular mass. Protein sequencing associated these bands with sodefrin precursor-like factors.

The study establishes secretion of candidate signaling proteins during courtship. It did not test each purified axolotl protein in a female behavioral assay. Courtship-associated release and molecular identification support a pheromone hypothesis without independently proving the behavioral function of every component.

slides.title: SPF proteins retain conserved sequence features
body: **Sodefrin precursor-like factor**, or SPF, names a family of candidate courtship proteins related by sequence and ancestry. Maex and colleagues combined cloacal RNA sequences with proteins recovered from axolotl courtship water, connecting predicted products with material actually secreted during the display.

Thirteen precursor sequences encoded twelve unique mature SPF proteins. Their **signal peptides**, short initial sequences associated with secretion, contained 20 amino acids. Conserved cysteine patterns distinguished alpha and beta SPF groups, while sequence differences identified multiple molecular variants.

A shared protein family does not guarantee identical behavioral action across salamander species. The sequence and secretion evidence establish candidate identity, not a purified-protein receptor response in a female axolotl. Conservation supports a comparative hypothesis while leaving species-specific function and effective concentration unresolved.

slides.title: A gland transcriptome identifies candidates for secretion
body: Hall and colleagues sequenced RNA from the cloacal gland of a male axolotl. A **homolog** is a sequence related to another through shared ancestry; an **ortholog** is a homolog separated by species divergence. Sequence comparisons identified candidates related to known salamander courtship-protein families.

The gland contained alpha and beta SPF transcripts and a candidate related to plethodontid modulating factor. Conserved amino-acid motifs supported these assignments. Beta SPF and the modulating-factor candidate had high transcript abundance within the sampled gland, but the analysis came from one individual.

RNA abundance does not directly establish secreted concentration, female receptor activation or a behavioral effect. The individual preparation also limits claims about population-wide variation. Protein recovery from water supplies complementary evidence of secretion, whereas purified-molecule behavioral assays would test the candidates’ specific signaling functions.

slides.title: Courtship modalities have different causal evidence
body: Axolotl courtship combines tail motion, proximity, contact and released chemicals. Mechanical nerve responses and courtship-water protein assays address different links in that interaction. Weak-field electroreception is established separately, but the cited studies do not demonstrate an electrical courtship signal.

Maex and colleagues detected 20–25-kDa SPF candidates in courtship water relative to noncourting controls. The Rupp preprint manipulated tail sweeps and speeds while providing male odorants, and recorded peripheral responses in a separate preparation. Its neural and behavioral findings have not been peer reviewed.

Together these results constrain a multimodal mechanism without identifying every channel, receptor or central integration site. Secretion is not equivalent to a purified pheromone effect, peripheral responsiveness is not behavioral necessity, and electrical detection is not evidence of social electrical communication. Each claim requires its own experimentally matched measurement.

Mechanical nerve responses and courtship-water protein assays address different links in that interaction. Weak-field electroreception is established separately, but the cited studies do not demonstrate an electrical courtship signal.

Maex and colleagues detected 20–25-kDa SPF candidates in courtship water relative to noncourting controls. The Rupp preprint manipulated tail sweeps and speeds while providing male odorants, and recorded peripheral responses in a separate preparation. Its neural and behavioral findings have not been peer reviewed.

The strongest integration preserves the distinction between what was manipulated and what was measured. No cited experiment simultaneously isolated chemical, mechanical and electrical cues while testing a complete central courtship circuit.

Together these results constrain a multimodal mechanism without identifying every channel, receptor or central integration site. Secretion is not equivalent to a purified pheromone effect, peripheral responsiveness is not behavioral necessity, and electrical detection is not evidence of social electrical communication. Each claim requires its own experimentally matched measurement.

items.text: Neuromasts detect water movement; ampullary organs support weak-field electroreception. Morphology, staining and physiological sensitivity provide complementary evidence.
Ear, mechanosensory and ampullary afferents appear in sequence and occupy ordered hindbrain territories. Timing is supported as a contributor, rather than proven as the sole sorting mechanism.
Weak-field afferents encode polarity and slow oscillations. Electrode voltage and local field strength are different quantities; increased locomotion alone is not source attraction.
Regional Kv expression and broad 4-AP effects support candidate mechanisms. They do not identify a subtype-specific current or prove an ampullary-cell-specific behavioral requirement.
Tectal sensory maps align only partly. Movement and several sensory inputs modulate outgoing lateral-line activity, without establishing a complete molecular feedback circuit.

SPF secretion and mechanical signaling have distinct experimental support. The Robotail findings are a preprint; electrical courtship signaling and individual SPF behavioral effects remain unestablished.
